parts.label: Part 1
parts.title: An important language development
parts.article:
An important language development
 
(A) Cuneiform, the world's first known system of handwriting, originated some 6,000 years ago in Sumer in what is now southern Iraq. It was most often inscribed on palm-sized, rectangular clay tablets measuring several centimetres across, although occasionally larger tablets or cylinders were used. Clay was an excellent medium for writing. Other surfaces which have been employed—for example, parchment, papyrus and paper—are not long lasting and are easily destroyed by fire and water. But clay has proved to be resistant to those particular kinds of damage. The word 'cuneiform' actually refers to the marks or signs inscribed in the clay. The original cuneiform signs consisted of a series of lines—triangular, vertical, diagonal, and horizontal. Sumerian writers would impress these lines into the wet clay with a stylus—a long, thin, pointed instrument which looked somewhat like a pen. Oddly, the signs were often almost too small to see with the naked eye. Cuneiform signs were used for the writing of at least a dozen languages. This is similar to how the Latin alphabet is used today for writing English, French, Spanish and German, for example.
 
(B) Before the development of cuneiform, tokens were used by the Sumerians to record certain information. For example, they might take small stones and use them as tokens or representations of something else, like a goat. A number of tokens, then, might mean a herd of goats. These tokens might then be placed in a cloth container and provided to a buyer as a receipt for a transaction, perhaps five tokens for five animals. It was not that different from what we do today when we buy some bread and the clerk gives us back a piece of paper with numbers on it to confirm the exchange. By the 4th century BCE, the Sumerians had adapted this system to a form of writing. They began putting tokens in a container resembling an envelope, one made of clay instead of cloth. They then stamped the outside to indicate the number and type of tokens inside. A person could then 'read' what was stamped on the container and know what was inside.
 
(C) Gradually, Sumerians developed symbols for words. When first developed, each symbol looked like the concrete thing it represented. For example, an image which resembled the drawing of a sheep meant just that. Then another level of abstraction was introduced when symbols were developed for intangible ideas such as 'female' or 'hot' or 'God'. Cuneiform, in other words, evolved from a way used primarily to track and store information into a way to represent the world symbolically. Over the centuries, the marks became ever more abstract, finally evolving into signs that looked nothing like what they referred to, just as the letters 'h-o-u-s-e' have no visual connection to the place we live in. At this last stage in the evolution of cuneiform, the signs took the form of triangles, which became common cuneiform signs. As the marks became more abstract, the system became more efficient because there were fewer marks for a 'reader' to learn. But cuneiform also became more complex because society itself was becoming more complex, so there were more ideas and concepts that needed to be expressed. However, most linguists and historians agree cuneiform developed primarily as a tool for accounting. Of the cuneiform tablets that have been discovered, excavated and translated, about 75 percent contain this type of practical information, rather than artistic or imaginative work.
 
(D) Cuneiform writing was used for thousands of years, but it eventually ceased to be used in everyday life. In fact, it died out and remained unintelligible for almost 2,000 years. In the late 19th century, a British army officer, Henry Rawlinson, discovered cuneiform inscriptions which had been carved into the surface of rocks in the Behistun Mountains in what is present-day Iran. Rawlinson made impressions of the marks on large pieces of paper as he balanced dangerously on the surrounding rocks. Rawlinson took his copies home to Britain and studied them for years to determine what each line stood for, and what each group of symbols meant. He found that, in the writing on those particular rocks, every word was repeated three times in three languages: Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. Since the meanings in these languages were already known to linguists, he could thus translate the cuneiform. Eventually, he fully decoded the cuneiform marks and discovered that they described the life of Darius, a king of the Persian Empire in the 5th century BCE.

questions.question: Cuneiform tablets were produced in different shapes and sizes.

analyses.content: “Rectangular... cylinders” 对应不同形状，“Palm-sized... larger” 对应不同尺寸。
(Paragraph A) “It was most often inscribed on palm-sized, rectangular clay tablets... although occasionally larger tablets or cylinders were used.”
题目说楔形文字泥板有不同的形状和尺寸。原文A段提到它通常刻在“palm-sized, rectangular（巴掌大小、长方形）”的泥板上，但有时也使用“larger tablets or cylinders（更大的泥板或圆柱体）”，即形状（长方vs圆柱）和尺寸（巴掌大vs更大）都不同，选 TRUE。

questions.question: When Sumerian writers marked the clay tablets, the tablets were dry.

analyses.content: 题目说苏美尔书写者在泥板上刻写时，泥板是干的（dry）。原文A段明确说书写者将线条压入“wet clay（湿黏土）”中，题目与原文相反，选 FALSE。
“Dry” 与原文的 “wet” 直接矛盾。
(Paragraph A) “Sumerian writers would impress these lines into the wet clay...”

questions.question: Cuneiform was often difficult to read because of its size.

analyses.content: 题目说楔形文字因其尺寸（size）而往往难以阅读。原文A段提到这些符号奇怪地“almost too small to see with the naked eye（几乎小到肉眼看不见）”，即因为太小而难读，选 TRUE。
“Difficult to read” 对应 “too small to see”。
(Paragraph A) “Oddly, the signs were often almost too small to see with the naked eye.”

questions.question: A number of languages adopted cuneiform.

analyses.content: “At least a dozen” 这是一个具体的数量，足以构成 “a number of”。
题目说**许多（a number of）**语言采用了楔形文字。原文A段提到楔形文字被用于书写“at least a dozen languages（至少一打/12种语言）”，符合“a number of”的描述，选 TRUE。
(Paragraph A) “Cuneiform signs were used for the writing of at least a dozen languages.”

questions.question: Cuneiform signs can be found in some modern alphabets.

analyses.content: 题目说楔形文字符号可以在一些现代字母表中找到。原文A段末尾虽然拿它和现代“Latin alphabet（拉丁字母表）”做类比（说用法相似，都是一种文字记录多种语言），但从未提及楔形文字符号本身存在于现代字母表中，且D段开头说它“died out（灭绝了）”，选 NOT GIVEN。
原文是“Similar to how... is used（用法相似）”，不是“Signs can be found in（符号存在于）”。
(Paragraph A) “This is similar to how the Latin alphabet is used today...” (仅作类比)

analyses.content: 题目说代币（tokens），例如____经常被使用。原文B段提到他们可能会拿小“stones（石头）”作为代币，填 stones。
“For example” 对应 “like” 或直接举例逻辑 “take small stones and use them as tokens”。
(Paragraph B) “For example, they might take small stones and use them as tokens...”
(Paragraph B) “These tokens might then be placed in a cloth container...”
“Made of” 对应 “cloth container”。
题目说最早的代币被保存在由____制成的容器里。原文B段提到这些代币会被放入一个“cloth container（布制容器）”中，填 cloth。
题目说代币被用作一种____，在卖东西时给出。原文B段提到代币作为交易的“receipt（收据）”提供给买家，填 receipt。
“To give when selling” 对应 “provided to a buyer... for a transaction”。
(Paragraph B) “...provided to a buyer as a receipt for a transaction...”
题目说代币被放入一个看起来像黏土____的容器中。原文B段提到他们开始把代币放入一个类似于“envelope（信封）”的容器，由黏土制成，填 envelope。
“Looked like” 对应 “resembling”。
(Paragraph B) “They began putting tokens in a container resembling an envelope...”
(Paragraph C) “For example, an image which resembled the drawing of a sheep meant just that.”
题目说起初符号看起来像它们所指示的事物，例如____。原文C段举例说一个类似“drawing of a sheep（羊的图画）”的图像就意味着羊，填 sheep。
“E.g.” 对应 “For example”。
题目说最终，形状像____的楔形文字符号被开发出来。原文C段提到在最后阶段，符号采取了“triangles（三角形）”的形式，填 triangles。
“Shaped like” 对应 “took the form of”。
(Paragraph C) “...the signs took the form of triangles...”
题目说根据专家，楔形文字主要用于____。原文C段提到大多数语言学家同意楔形文字主要发展为一种“tool for accounting（记账工具）”，填 accounting。
“Mainly used for” 对应 “developed primarily as a tool for”。
(Paragraph C) “...cuneiform developed primarily as a tool for accounting.”
题目说Rawlinson将铭文复制到了____上。原文D段提到Rawlinson在岩石上平衡时，将标记的印记制作在“large pieces of paper（大张的纸）”上，填 paper。
“Copied... onto” 对应 “made impressions... on”。
(Paragraph D) “Rawlinson made impressions of the marks on large pieces of paper...”
